lessons.title: Removing shoes and assessing wear
lessons.html:
Safety and preparation

Shoeing is skilled, physical work. In this unit you work under the supervision of a qualified farrier. Wear a farrier's apron, safety boots, and safety glasses when grinding or working hot metal. Work on a level, clean, non-slip surface with good light. Make sure the horse is held by a competent handler or tied with a quick-release knot, and that it is standing square and calm.

Tools for removing shoes

  • Clench cutter (buffer) and driving hammer - to open the clenches
  • Shoe pullers (pull-offs) - to lever the shoe off
  • Crease nail puller - to pull individual nails
  • Rasp - to remove clench ends

Removing the shoe

  1. Pick out the foot and brush off dirt.
  2. Place the clench cutter under each clench and tap with the hammer to straighten (open) it, or rasp the clenches off.
  3. Grip one heel of the shoe with the pullers and lever towards the toe, inwards towards the centre of the foot, not outwards which can tear the wall.
  4. Repeat on the other heel and work alternately along both branches until the nails lift.
  5. Where possible pull the nails individually with the crease nail puller to reduce damage to the wall.
  6. Remove all old nails and nail stubs. Count the nails against the holes in the shoe.
  7. Put the foot down and place the old shoe and nails safely in a box, never on the ground where the horse can tread on them.

Assessing wear and the foot

The old shoe and the foot tell you how the horse moves and how the foot has grown.

ObservationPossible meaning
Even wear on both branchesBalanced foot and movement
Heavy wear on one branchMedio-lateral imbalance or a gait pattern
Excessive toe wearToe dragging, possibly long toe or a lameness problem
Shoe has moved, heels pressing on soleShoe left on too long; risk of corns
Loose or broken nailsOverdue shoeing or poor nailing

Look at the foot: length of toe, heel height, cracks, flares, the condition of the white line, thrush in the frog, bruising and corns. Watch the horse walk and trot on a hard surface. Report signs of lameness or disease to the farrier and owner; some conditions need a vet.

lessons.title: Trimming the foot
lessons.html:
Goals of the trim

A trim removes excess growth so the foot is balanced: the hoof is level side to side, the hoof wall angle lines up with the pastern, and the weight is borne evenly. A correct trim is the foundation of good shoeing; a shoe cannot correct a badly trimmed foot.

Tools

  • Hoof knife - pares sole and frog
  • Hoof nippers - cut the excess wall
  • Rasp - levels and finishes the bearing surface
  • Hoof gauge and T-square (optional) - check angles and level

Steps

  1. Clean the foot and look at the sole surface.
  2. Pare the sole: remove only flaky, dead sole with the knife until you reach live, waxy sole. Do not thin the sole; a thin sole bruises.
  3. Trim the frog: remove only loose tags and diseased tissue. A healthy frog helps absorb shock.
  4. Nip the wall: cut the excess wall evenly around the foot, starting at one heel and working round, leaving a little extra to rasp.
  5. Rasp the bearing surface level, using flat, full strokes. Check side-to-side balance by sighting down the foot or with a T-square.
  6. Check the hoof-pastern axis: viewed from the side, the front of the hoof wall and the front of the pastern should form a straight line. A broken-back axis often means the toe is too long or heels too low.
  7. Dress flares lightly from the outside of the wall; do not rasp the outer wall more than needed.

Safety for the horse

  • Never cut into the sensitive structures; bleeding means you have gone too far. Stop and inform the farrier.
  • Hold the leg in a comfortable, natural position; old horses and young horses may need more rests.
  • Keep sharp knives sheathed or in the tool box when not in use, and always cut away from yourself and the horse.

Barefoot horses

Some horses are kept unshod. Their trim leaves a slightly rounded edge (a "mustang roll") to prevent chipping. Discuss the plan with the farrier.

lessons.title: Fitting, nailing and finishing the shoe
lessons.html:
Choosing and shaping the shoe

Choose a shoe of the right size, weight and type for the horse's work and foot. Shape it to fit the trimmed foot, not the foot to fit the shoe. Shoes are shaped cold on the anvil, or hot after heating in the forge.

Correct fit

  • The shoe follows the outline of the wall around the toe and quarters.
  • Heels are long enough to support the back of the foot, extending slightly beyond the bearing surface, and fitted with a little width ("fullness") at the heels.
  • Nail holes line up with the white line.
  • The shoe sits flat on the foot with no gaps.

In hot fitting, keep contact between the hot shoe and foot brief, and cool the shoe before nailing.

Nailing

  1. Choose nails of the right size for the shoe and foot.
  2. Start the first nail at the toe area on one side, so the shoe can still be adjusted, then the opposite side.
  3. Drive each nail so it enters at the white line and exits the wall at an even height, angled outwards.
  4. As each nail comes through, bend the point over or twist it off to protect yourself and the handler.

Warning signs: if the horse flinches, pulls away or the nail sounds or feels different as you drive it, stop. The nail may be too close to the sensitive tissue (a "close" nail) or in it (a "prick"). Pull it out and tell the farrier at once. A prick can cause serious infection; the vet may be needed and the horse's tetanus status checked.

Clenching

  1. Cut the nail ends with the clench cutter, leaving enough to form a clench.
  2. Rasp a small groove under each nail end, or use a clench block.
  3. Turn the ends over with the clenchers so each clench lies flat in the wall.
  4. Rasp the clenches smooth so there are no sharp edges.

Finishing

Lightly rasp the wall where it meets the shoe so there is no overhang; do not rasp the wall heavily above the clenches, as this weakens it. Check the finished foot from the front, side and below. Watch the horse walk and trot to confirm it is sound. Record the work done and any findings.

Key points

  • Remove shoes by working pullers from the heels towards the toe, inwards; count every nail.
  • Assess shoe wear and the foot for balance, cracks, corns and lameness.
  • Trim to balance: pare dead sole only, level the wall, align the hoof-pastern axis.
  • Shape the shoe to the foot; nails enter at the white line and exit evenly.
  • Stop at once if the horse flinches while nailing; clench flat and finish smooth.

quiz.question: In which direction should shoe pullers be levered?

options.text: From the heels towards the toe, inwards
From the toe to the heels, outwards

quiz.question: Heavy wear on one branch of the old shoe may indicate what?

options.text: Medio-lateral imbalance or a gait pattern

quiz.question: When paring the sole, what should you remove?
What should the hoof-pastern axis look like from the side?
Where should a horseshoe nail enter the foot?

options.text: In the middle of the sole

quiz.question: The foot should be trimmed to fit the shoe, not the shoe shaped to fit the foot.
If the horse flinches while a nail is driven, you should stop and remove the nail.
Which are part of finishing the shoeing process? (select all that apply)

options.text: Cutting nail ends and forming clenches
Watching the horse walk and trot
Rasping the whole outer wall heavily
